Broided
BROY-ded
verb (past participle), adjective
The older English form of braided, from the Saxon bregdan, to weave or plait. Not to be confused with embroidered, which is needlework upon cloth; broided hair is hair plaited and interwoven, in the ancient fashion, commonly with gold thread and pearls worked into the braid.

Biblical Definition

The word stands in Paul’s instruction on the adorning of women: “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” (1Ti 2:9). The context governs the meaning. In the Ephesus of that day the elaborately plaited coiffure, worked through with gold wire and pearls, was the recognised display of a wealthy woman — expensive, time-consuming, and unmistakably a statement of rank. Paul is not forbidding a plait as such, any more than Peter forbids the wearing of apparel when he writes against “plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel” (1Pe 3:3), for a woman who obeyed that literally would go out unclothed. Both apostles are naming the ostentatious style of their own day in order to strike at the heart behind it. And both immediately supply the substitute, which is the point. Paul says the adorning that becomes women professing godliness is “good works” (1Ti 2:10); Peter says it is the hidden man of the heart, the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The command is not wear less but adorn yourself with something better, and the standard of value named is God’s own estimate.

Webster 1828 Definition

Plaited or braided, as hair interwoven in strands; in the apostolic warning, the elaborate and costly coiffure worked with gold and pearls.

BROID, v.t. The older form of braid: to weave or plait together, as strands of hair.

From the Saxon bregdan, to weave, to plait, to draw together.

Distinguished from embroider, which is ornamental needlework upon a fabric.

BROIDED, pp. Plaited; interwoven; as, broided hair (1Ti 2:9).

In antiquity, such plaiting was frequently interwoven with gold thread and pearls.

Key Scripture

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

1Ti 2:10 — "But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works."

1Pe 3:3 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;"

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Modern Corruption

The text is pulled in two wrong directions at once — made into a rulebook against braids and jewellery by the strict, and dismissed as cultural residue by the progressive — while the apostolic argument, that adorning is real and must be relocated, is lost by both.

expand to see more

The corruption runs two ways, and the dictionary rejects both. On one side, the legalist reads 1Ti 2:9 as a dress code and produces rules about braids, jewellery, and hemlines that Scripture never gave, making a woman’s godliness measurable by what she has removed. Peter’s parallel exposes the method at once: the same grammar that forbids plaited hair forbids putting on of apparel, and no one supposes the Apostle commanded nakedness. On the other side, progressive readers file the passage under first-century custom and let it say nothing at all — a method which, applied consistently, empties every apostolic instruction on the ground that it was written to somebody in particular. Both evade the same sentence, because both find it easier to argue about hair than about the heart it advertises.

Recover the plain sense: the apostles do not abolish adorning, they relocate it. Every woman will be adorned by something; the question is what she is trusting to make her admired, and at whose expense. Paul answers good works, Peter answers the meek and quiet spirit which is in the sight of God of great price. Note that both give a market valuation. Costly array is costly by the world’s reckoning; the hidden man of the heart is costly by God’s, and He is the buyer whose price stands. That principle judges the wealthy woman’s pearls and the austere woman’s conspicuous plainness with equal force, since a severity displayed for admiration is only broided hair by another name.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon bregdan, to plait — interwoven hair; the apostolic call to relocate adorning from the head to the heart.

Broided — older form of braided; Saxon bregdan, to weave or plait.

Distinct from embroidered, which is needlework upon cloth.

Anciently plaited with gold thread and pearls as a display of rank.

1Ti 2:10 supplies the substitute: good works.

1Pe 3:4 names the price: a meek and quiet spirit, of great price with God.

Usage

"Peter’s parallel forbids putting on of apparel in the same breath — the sense is comparative, not absolute."

"Both apostles name a replacement adorning; neither leaves the woman unadorned."

"Conspicuous plainness adopted for admiration is broided hair under another name."
